In the same month, three things fell on Raghav. He failed his second-year accounts paper. His father, who ran a small grocery in their town in Madhya Pradesh, was admitted with a heart problem. And the shop's takings dropped because nobody was there to open it.
Raghav stopped going to college. He opened the shop at seven, visited the hospital at lunch, and sat up at night staring at his textbook without reading.
Manoj Sir, his accounts lecturer, came to the shop one evening to buy soap and saw his face. "You've disappeared," he said gently.
Raghav told him everything, fast, like it was spilling out.
Manoj Sir didn't offer speeches. He told Raghav about the college's supplementary exam and the fee concession form, and gave him the counsellor's number. He also suggested asking his cousin to take one shift at the shop.
Raghav filled the form the next morning. It didn't fix everything. But he wasn't carrying it alone anymore.

qa.a: His father would probably feel worried and guilty, but relieved that a teacher and family were helping.

In Mexico City, Alejandro was in his final year of engineering when his mother was diagnosed with a serious illness. He took extra shifts at a café to cover bus fares to the hospital and his younger sister's school costs. His grades slid. He stopped replying to his friend Emil.
One night Emil turned up at the café at closing time. "You look like you haven't slept in weeks."
"I haven't," Alejandro said, and to his own surprise, his voice broke.
They sat on the curb. Emil asked what help existed, not what Alejandro should do. Together they found that the university had an emergency student fund and a counselling service, and that professors could grant deadline extensions for family illness.
The next morning Alejandro emailed two professors and booked a counselling slot. He still worked the café shifts. But now he had a plan, and someone who knew.

qa.a: It suggests Alejandro was exhausted and overwhelmed, finally letting out the stress he'd been hiding.

qa.a: Most would likely feel sympathetic and grant extensions, relieved to know why his work had slipped.

Mentor's note. Sarika, team lead, product design.
Dolma, 24, asked me last month how to get promoted. I told her the truth: she does excellent work, but nobody outside our team knows it, and she never asks for feedback.
She took it seriously. She started asking after every project, "What's one thing I could have done better?" She wrote down the answers, even the harsh ones, and I saw her wince at a couple. She also asked if I'd introduce her to Arun from the strategy team, who sits on promotion panels. She presented her research at his team meeting.
At our last check-in, we wrote a growth plan together: skills to build, projects to lead, and a review date in six months.
She's still quiet in big meetings. But her name comes up now when leaders talk about who's ready.

qa.a: "What's one thing I could have done better?"

qa.a: It suggests Dolma felt hurt and uncomfortable at times, but kept asking because she wanted to grow.

qa.q: Which steps in Dolma's approach could help others plan their growth?
qa.a: Asking for specific feedback, building a sponsor who sits on promotion panels, showing work to other teams and writing a plan with a review date.

Friday
Karthik writing. Two years at this company. Performance review today: "meets expectations". I was sure I'd get "exceeds". Came home and sulked through dinner.
Then I called Vishal Sir, my old manager, who moved to another division. He didn't sugarcoat it. "Do you know what your manager thinks 'exceeds' looks like?" I didn't. I'd never asked.
He told me three things:
Ask your manager for specific examples of what the next level does.
Ask for feedback every month, not once a year.
Find someone senior who knows your work and will speak for you when you're not in the room.
It stung that I'd been waiting to be noticed instead of asking. On Monday, I'm booking a thirty-minute chat with my manager, with those questions written down.

qa.q: What was Karthik's performance rating?
qa.a: "Meets expectations".

qa.q: How did Karthik feel after the review?
qa.a: Karthik felt disappointed and sulky, having expected "exceeds".

qa.q: Which of Vishal Sir's three tips would you advise Karthik to start with, and why?
qa.a: Asking the manager for specific examples of the next level, because it makes the goal clear before anything else.

qa.q: How might Karthik's manager see the chat on Monday?
qa.a: The manager would probably appreciate the initiative and find it easier to guide someone who asks directly.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional learning to seek specific feedback and a sponsor to plan career growth.

Vidya's diary. Three weeks as team lead and I've made every mistake.
I've been doing everything myself because it's faster. My team of four looks bored. Arohi, the newest, asked yesterday if she'd done something wrong because I'd rewritten her report without saying anything. I felt awful.

At twenty-five, Ishita became manager of a small bank branch in a town in Himachal, with a team of five, most of them older than her. Chinmay, the youngest clerk, was friendly but slow with loan files, and customers had started complaining.
She didn't scold him at the counter. After closing, she asked him to stay for tea. "The loan files are taking too long. Two customers complained this week. I want to help fix it. Where do you get stuck?"
Chinmay was quiet. Then he admitted he was scared of making mistakes, so he checked everything three times.
Ishita sat with him and made a simple checklist for each file. For two weeks, she checked his first file each morning, then stepped back. She also gave the senior clerk the task of mentoring him.
By the end of the month Chinmay's files were on time. At the staff meeting, Ishita thanked him in front of everyone.

qa.q: How many customers complained that week?
qa.a: Two customers.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling that made him slow?
qa.a: Chinmay felt scared of making mistakes, so he checked everything three times.

qa.q: Which of Ishita's choices were good people management?
qa.a: She raised the issue privately and plainly, asked where he got stuck, gave a checklist, coached then stepped back, and praised him publicly.

qa.q: How might the older team members see Ishita after this?
qa.a: They might respect her more, seeing she handles problems fairly and helps people improve.

grounding: Illustrates a young manager coaching a junior, delegating mentoring and delivering hard feedback with respect.

When I got my first offer after my master's, I almost said yes on the phone. The HR person said a number, and I felt so grateful to be picked that I wanted to accept before they changed their minds.
My friend Ojas, who'd negotiated his own offer, stopped me. "Ask for a day. Then do your homework."
So I did. I looked up salary surveys for the role and city, and asked two seniors what they'd been offered. The number was at the bottom of the range.
I rehearsed with Ojas. The next day I said, "I'm really excited about this role. Based on the market range and my project experience, I was hoping for something closer to the middle of the range." My voice shook a bit.
They came back with a higher offer and an extra review after six months. I'm Yash, and I learned that asking politely isn't greedy.

qa.q: What did Ojas tell Yash to ask for first?
qa.a: A day, to do some homework.

qa.q: How did Yash feel when the first number was offered?
qa.a: Yash felt grateful and eager, so relieved at being picked that saying yes immediately was tempting.

qa.q: Which parts of Yash's preparation made the negotiation work without damaging the relationship?
qa.a: Researching the market, rehearsing, starting with enthusiasm and giving reasons for the request kept it polite and grounded.

qa.q: How might the HR person have seen Yash's request?
qa.a: The HR person probably saw it as normal and professional, since it was polite and based on market data.

Hiring manager's note. Darshan, operations lead.
We offered Jomon, 25, a team coordinator role. He thanked us and asked for two days. When he came back, he was prepared.
He didn't just ask for more money. He said he was excited about the role, then explained that his current job included managing vendors, which our role also needs, and that similar roles in the city paid more. He named a figure a little above what we'd planned, clearly as a starting point.
When I said the budget was fixed, he asked about other terms: a review after six months, two work-from-home days, and a training allowance. He stayed friendly the whole time.
We couldn't meet his figure, but we agreed on part of the gap, the six-month review and the training. I came away respecting him more, not less. I think he'll negotiate well with our vendors too.

qa.a: Two days.

qa.a: Jomon likely felt nervous but confident, having prepared his reasons and alternatives.

qa.a: Jomon anchored with a researched figure, linked it to his experience, stayed friendly, and moved to other terms when salary was fixed.
